risks.risk: Execution and project delivery risk on complex shipbuilding projects

This is the dominant risk for a company whose entire near-term value rests on delivering a newly won order book.

risks.risk: Dependence on imported equipment and components
risks.note: Critical marine equipment, propulsion systems, navigation systems and specialised components continue to have import dependency, exposing the business to currency fluctuations, supply disruptions and procurement delays.

risks.risk: Raw material price volatility on fixed-price contracts
risks.note: Fluctuations in prices of steel, specialty alloys and marine equipment can adversely impact project margins, particularly on fixed-price contracts - the contract form used for the vessel orders in hand.

Evolving global regulations on emissions, vessel efficiency, environmental standards and safety compliance may require continuous operational and technological upgrades, i.e. recurring compliance capex and design rework.

The MD&A states the Company is a single segment company, so there is no segmental diversification to absorb a downturn or an execution problem in shipbuilding.

one_liner.title: One Liner (RHP)
one_liner.body: Swan Defence and Heavy Industries Limited (formerly Reliance Naval and Engineering Limited) is an integrated Indian shipyard building commercial and defence vessels and undertaking ship repair, refit and offshore fabrication, operating as a single-segment company.

business_model.title: What they do
business_model.body: SDHI operates an integrated shipyard that constructs commercial vessels (chemical tankers and dual-fuel ammonia bulk carriers) and defence vessels (a naval training ship for the Royal Navy of Oman), and also undertakes ship repair and refit assignments. Customers span international commercial shipowners and foreign government defence buyers, alongside the Indian maritime and defence ecosystem. The Company acquired the shipyard through a corporate insolvency resolution process and describes itself as a single segment company.

group_structure.title: Group structure (subsidiaries / JV / related parties)
group_structure.body:

- Hazel Infra Limited — related party: Immediate Holding Company; unsecured loan relationship with the Company
- Reliance Technologies and Systems Private Limited (RTSPL) — subsidiary: Listed as an ongoing subsidiary company in the related-party note

The Company continues to hold 100% of ECPL's equity but has assessed it does not have control under Ind AS 110, so ECPL is not treated as a related party under Ind AS 24; the investment has been impaired

products.title: Products & brands
products.body:
- **Commercial shipbuilding:** 18,000 DWT IMO Type II chemical tankers, 92,500 DWT dual-fuel ammonia bulk carriers
- **Defence shipbuilding:** State-of-the-art naval training ship (Royal Navy of Oman)
- **Ship repair and marine services:** Ship repair and refit assignments

end_markets.title: End Markets (RHP)
end_markets.body:
- International commercial shipowners (Rederiet Stenersen AS, Norway; Energy ONE Limited)
- Defence exports - Government of the Sultanate of Oman / Royal Navy of Oman
- Indian shipbuilding, defence and maritime sector
- Ship repair and refit customers

demand_drivers.title: Demand & outlook drivers
demand_drivers.body:
- Government policy push: a shipbuilding package of Rs 69,725 Crore approved in September 2025 comprising SBFAS, the Maritime Development Fund and the Shipbuilding Development Scheme, with SBFAS 2.0 backed by a dedicated allocation of Rs 24,736 Crore through 2036
- Infrastructure status notified on 19th September 2025 for Indian-flagged commercial vessels of 10,000 GT or above, and for India-built vessels of 1,500 GT or above
- Demand aggregation: a fleet acquisition plan for more than 400 vessels prepared, providing long-term order visibility for Indian shipyards
- Global fleet replacement cycle: over 40% of the global merchant fleet is over 20 years of age, with ageing tonnage reaching 25 years projected to accelerate from nearly 28 million GT to almost 100 million GT by 2035
- Capacity scarcity at tier-1 Asian yards - an average order backlog of 4.4 years and next dry-dock availability beyond 4 years - shifting international demand toward Indian yards
- Domestic PSU order pipeline: a Government procurement programme for 437 vessels estimated at Rs 2.2 lakh crore over the next decade, with Shipping Corporation of India as nodal aggregating agency
- Defence procurement: the Indian Navy's frontline combat fleet projected to expand by 80% by FY 2029-30, creating a multi-year pipeline across frigates, destroyers, submarines and auxiliary vessels
- Green shipping transition driving demand for LNG-powered, dual-fuel, hybrid and ammonia-ready vessels under IMO decarbonisation targets
- Global shipbuilding market projected to expand from USD 175.71 billion in 2026 to USD 274.19 billion by 2034, a CAGR of 5.72%
- A 25% capital subsidy for brownfield expansion and infrastructure modernisation available to existing shipyards under the Shipbuilding Development Scheme
- Management headwinds flagged: subsidised competition from Chinese, South Korean and Japanese yards, execution and delivery risk on complex projects, import dependency for critical marine equipment, raw material price volatility on fixed-price contracts
- The confirmed shipbuilding order book currently comprises multiple active orders across commercial and defence categories
- USD 227 million contract with Rederiet Stenersen AS, Norway, for six 18,000 DWT IMO Type II chemical tankers - described as one of India's largest commercial shipbuilding contracts and the first chemical tanker order awarded to an Indian shipyard, with an option for six additional vessels
- Order for four 92,500 DWT dual-fuel ammonia bulk carriers from Energy ONE Limited
- Defence export order from the Government of the Sultanate of Oman for a state-of-the-art training vessel for the Royal Navy of Oman, currently under execution
- Ship repair and refit assignments undertaken and completed during the year
- This was the Company's first major commercial shipbuilding order following acquisition of the shipyard through CIRP

capital_allocation.title: Strategy & capital allocation
capital_allocation.body:
- Timely execution of the existing order book as the stated first priority for FY 2026-27
- Expanding presence across commercial shipbuilding, defence, ship repair and offshore fabrication, plus green vessel segments
- Building a globally competitive shipbuilding platform through strategic collaborations and MoUs with Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers, Royal IHC, Samsung Heavy Industries and Fincantieri
- Positioning in next-generation green vessels (dual-fuel ammonia carriers) to capture IMO decarbonisation-led demand
- Growing the defence and defence-export franchise, having secured a naval training vessel order from the Government of the Sultanate of Oman
- Balance-sheet clean-up: concluding the CIRP by prepaying all Committee of Creditors obligations to create a de-leveraged base for scaling operations
- Corporate simplification via a Scheme of Arrangement and Amalgamation of Triumph Offshore Private Limited into SDHI, including reduction and re-organisation of the Transferee Company's capital
- Strengthening the internal financial control framework through process formalisation, system automation and enhanced documentation
- Workforce build-out and skill development in welding, erection, profiling and specialised shipbuilding disciplines
- The report states policy intent rather than a payout philosophy: in terms of Regulation 43A of the SEBI Listing Regulations the Company has adopted a Dividend Distribution Policy, available on its website, and it also maintains a structured Risk Management Policy designed to anticipate, evaluate and mitigate risks, plus a Board-approved policy framework on related party transactions with all RPTs during the year stated to be in the ordinary course of business and on an arm's length basis. No dividend quantum, payout ratio, buyback or reinvestment target is stated in this material.

capex_expansion.title: Capex & expansion plans
capex_expansion.body: The annual report describes no new named capex project with a commissioning or completion timeline; expansion is framed as capability and utilisation of the existing integrated shipyard rather than a greenfield build-out. The Company states it operates the largest dry dock in India, 662 metres long and 65 metres wide, allowing simultaneous construction of large vessels, an annual fabrication capacity of 1,64,000 metric tonnes with fabrication sheds capable of producing modular blocks weighing up to 300 tonnes, a large-scale semi-automated TTS panel production line, and dedicated pre-outfitting and mega block assembly areas served by a 600 MT Goliath crane. Growth capacity is described as 'available capacity' within this existing infrastructure, to be filled by the order book - six 18,000 DWT chemical tankers for Rederiet Stenersen AS (USD 227 million, with an option for six more vessels), four 92,500 DWT dual-fuel ammonia bulk carriers for Energy ONE Limited, and a naval training vessel for the Royal Navy of Oman. During the year the Company focused on operational improvements, workforce development, infrastructure optimization and process enhancement across the shipyard, and concluded its CIRP by prepaying all Committee of Creditors obligations originally scheduled for December 2026 and 2027, which it says establishes a de-leveraged balance sheet allowing the shipyard to scale up operations. At an industry level the report notes that under the Shipbuilding Development Scheme existing shipyards are eligible for a 25% capital subsidy for brownfield expansion and infrastructure modernisation; the Company does not state that it has claimed or applied for this. The Capital Commitments named-disclosure block supplied carries only the caption 'Estimated amount of contracts remaining to be executed on Capital Account and not provided for' with no figure attached, so no rupee capex quantum is available.

moat.title: Bull — competitive strengths
moat.body:
- Operates the largest dry dock in India, 662 metres long and 65 metres wide, enabling simultaneous construction of large vessels
- Annual fabrication capacity of 1,64,000 metric tonnes, with fabrication sheds able to produce modular blocks weighing up to 300 tonnes
- Advanced automation including a large-scale semi-automated TTS panel production line
- Dedicated pre-outfitting and mega block assembly areas served by a 600 MT Goliath crane
- Experienced leadership under CEO Rear Admiral Vipin Kumar Saxena (Retd), with naval architects, marine engineers and defence production experts
- Diversified order book across commercial and defence categories - chemical tankers, dual-fuel ammonia bulk carriers, naval training vessels and ship repair
- Strategic collaborations with Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers, Royal IHC, Samsung Heavy Industries and Fincantieri
- De-leveraged balance sheet following prepayment of all Committee of Creditors obligations and closure of the resolution plan

risks.title: Bear — key risks
risks.body:
- Global competition from subsidised shipyards — International shipyards, particularly in China, South Korea and Japan, benefit from significant government subsidies, making it challenging for Indian yards to compete on pricing and delivery timelines - a structural pricing disadvantage for a yard bidding for international contracts.
- Execution and project delivery risk on complex shipbuilding projects — Large, technically complex builds involve stringent delivery schedules, multi-vendor coordination and engineering integration challenges, which management says may impact execution timelines and project profitability. This is the dominant risk for a company whose entire near-term value rests on delivering a newly won order book.
- Dependence on imported equipment and components — Critical marine equipment, propulsion systems, navigation systems and specialised components continue to have import dependency, exposing the business to currency fluctuations, supply disruptions and procurement delays.
- Raw material price volatility on fixed-price contracts — Fluctuations in prices of steel, specialty alloys and marine equipment can adversely impact project margins, particularly on fixed-price contracts - the contract form used for the vessel orders in hand.
- Changing international maritime regulatory frameworks — Evolving global regulations on emissions, vessel efficiency, environmental standards and safety compliance may require continuous operational and technological upgrades, i.e. recurring compliance capex and design rework.
- Natural disasters and climate risk at a coastal facility — Operations near coastal areas are exposed to weather-related disruptions such as cyclones, flooding or heavy monsoons, affecting project schedules.
- Single-segment concentration — The MD&A states the Company is a single segment company, so there is no segmental diversification to absorb a downturn or an execution problem in shipbuilding.
- Internal financial control framework still being built out — Management describes FY 2025-26 as a year of strengthening and formalising internal financial controls alongside expanding operational scale, and states that while the controls in place are considered adequate, 'further improvements are ongoing' - a control-maturity gap relative to the step-up in scale.

strategy.body:

- Building a globally competitive shipbuilding platform through strategic collaborations and MoUs with Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders, Garden Reach Shipbuilders & Engineers, Royal IHC, Samsung Heavy Industries and Fincantieri
